title: Science in the kitchen: how cooking changes rice, butter and milk

summary.text: Ten grains of boiled rice make a much longer line than ten dry grains. Your child soaks some grains in cold water and boils others for the same time, and finds that heat lets the water go deep inside each grain. Then they melt a spoon of butter and watch it set again, while a grown-up heats another spoon until it becomes ghee, which never turns back into butter. They also find out how tiny living beings called bacteria turn milk into curd. Some kitchen changes can go back, and some stay changed for ever.
summary.art: A strip of paper on a kitchen counter with three lines of ten rice grains each: a short line of dry grains, a slightly longer line of white soaked grains, and a long line of fat, soft boiled grains.

intro.hook: Put one dry grain of rice next to one grain of cooked rice from lunch. Which one is bigger? Where did the extra come from?
intro.text: Every day, cooking changes the food in your kitchen. Hard rice turns soft. Butter turns runny in a warm pan. Milk turns into thick curd overnight. In this unit you test what heat and water do to rice grains. You melt butter and watch a grown-up turn butter into ghee. You find out who really sets the curd. And you sort kitchen changes into ones that can go back and ones that cannot.
intro.art: A girl of seven looking through a magnifying glass at one dry rice grain and one cooked rice grain on a steel plate.

outcomes: By the end I can say how cooking changes rice: the grains take in water and grow long and soft.
By the end I can show that rice takes in much more water in boiling water than in cold water.
By the end I can show that melted butter sets again when it is cold, and say why ghee does not turn back into butter.
By the end I can say that tiny living beings called bacteria turn milk into curd.
By the end I can sort kitchen changes into ones that can go back and ones that stay changed.
By the end I can line up and compare grains, and say what I think, what I saw and why.

terms.meaning: Cooking is changing food, usually with heat, so that it is soft, safe and good to eat.
terms.example: Boiling rice, frying a dosa and roasting groundnuts are all cooking.
terms.art: A gas stove with a pan of boiling rice, a dosa on a tawa and groundnuts roasting in a kadai.

terms.meaning: To absorb means to take something in, the way a sponge takes in water.
terms.example: Rice grains absorb water when they cook, so they get bigger and softer.
terms.art: A dry kitchen sponge next to a fat, wet sponge, and a dry rice grain next to a fat cooked grain.

terms.meaning: Starch is the main part of a rice grain. It is a store of food that the rice plant made.
terms.example: Rice, ragi, wheat and potatoes are full of starch.
terms.art: A heap of rice, a ragi ball, a chapati and a potato on a steel plate.

terms.meaning: To melt means to change from a solid into a liquid when something gets warm.
terms.example: Butter melts on hot dosa and runs down the sides.
terms.art: A blob of butter melting on a hot dosa, with a yellow trickle running off the edge.

terms.meaning: To set means to go firm or solid. Butter sets when it gets cold. Curd sets when milk turns thick.
terms.example: Coconut oil sets white in the bottle on a cold morning.
terms.art: A clear bottle of coconut oil, half white and solid at the bottom, on a winter windowsill.

terms.meaning: Ghee is butter that has been heated until its water has bubbled away as steam. It is almost all fat.
terms.example: Many families make ghee at home from butter (vennai in Tamil, makkhan in Hindi).
terms.art: A small steel kadai of golden ghee with a few light brown bits at the bottom.

terms.meaning: Bacteria are tiny living beings, far too small to see. Some of them live in curd.
terms.example: Bacteria in a spoon of curd turn a whole bowl of warm milk into curd by morning.
terms.art: A katori of curd with a round zoom-in bubble showing many tiny rod-shaped bacteria.

terms.term: A change that can go back
terms.meaning: A change that can be undone, so the thing becomes what it was before. Scientists call it a reversible change.
terms.example: Melted butter goes back to solid butter in the fridge.
terms.art: Two arrows in a circle between a solid blob of butter and a puddle of melted butter.

explanations.definition: Cooking changes how food looks, feels, smells and tastes, usually by heating it.
explanations.description: Raw rice is hard and dry. After boiling, it is soft, white and bigger. A dosa starts as runny batter and ends as a crisp, brown circle. Heat does most of these changes, and cooking makes many foods easier to chew and digest.
examples: Raw dal is hard. Cooked dal is soft enough to mash with a spoon.
Runny dosa batter on a hot tawa turns into a firm dosa in a few minutes.
Hard maize kernels pop into fluffy popcorn in a hot pan.
explanations.context: This card says what cooking does to food.
explanations.art: Three before-and-after pairs in a row: raw rice and cooked rice, dosa batter and a dosa, maize kernels and popcorn.

explanations.concept: Rice absorbs water when it cooks
explanations.definition: When rice cooks in hot water, the starch inside each grain absorbs water and swells, so the grain gets longer, fatter and softer.
explanations.description: A dry rice grain is hard because its starch is packed tight. In cold water, only a little water gets in, so the grain turns a little whiter but stays hard. In boiling water, the heat loosens the packed starch. Now water can go deep inside, and the grain swells. One cup of rice with two cups of water fills about three cups when cooked.
examples: Ten boiled grains in a line are about one and a half times as long as ten dry grains. Long grains like basmati can grow to nearly twice as long.
Soaked rice, used for idli and dosa batter, is white and a little bigger, but still hard.
When rice cooks, the water in the pan goes down, because the grains drink it.
explanations.context: This card explains what you saw in the ten-grain test.
explanations.art: A zoom-in of one rice grain: on the left, tightly packed starch grains; on the right, the same grains swollen and loose, with water drops between them.

explanations.concept: Butter melts and sets again, but ghee stays ghee
explanations.definition: Butter melts when warm and sets again when cold. Heated for longer, its water boils away and it becomes ghee, which cannot turn back into butter.
explanations.description: Butter is mostly fat, with some water and a little milk mixed in. Warm it gently, and the fat melts. Cool it, and the fat sets again. Heat butter longer, and it fizzes. That sound is the water in the butter boiling away as steam. What is left is ghee, and the water cannot come back.
examples: Butter on hot rice melts, and sets again if the rice gets cold.
Ghee is runny in a Chennai summer and goes solid and grainy on a cold Delhi morning. Both of those changes go back.
The brown bits at the bottom of a ghee pan are the milk parts of the butter, cooked by the heat.
explanations.context: This card explains the butter test, where one spoon melted and one became ghee.
explanations.art: Two steel katoris: one of pale yellow butter that has set again, and one of golden ghee with tiny brown bits at the bottom.

explanations.definition: Tiny living beings called bacteria eat the sugar in milk and make an acid. The acid makes the milk thick and sour. That is curd.
explanations.description: Curd is made by bacteria, not by heat. A spoon of curd holds millions of them. In warm milk, they feed on the milk sugar and make an acid, which tastes sour. The acid makes the milk thick, so by morning the whole bowl has set. Cold slows the bacteria down, so milk in the fridge stays runny.
examples: Families all over India set curd at night, from a spoon of the day's curd, to eat with rice the next day.
Curd rice in Tamil Nadu, mishti doi in Bengal and chaas in Gujarat all start with bacteria working on milk.
Idli and dosa batter rise overnight because tiny living beings work in the batter too.
explanations.context: This card is about how milk becomes curd.
explanations.art: A katori of milk at night and the same katori of thick curd in the morning, with a moon and a sun above them.

explanations.concept: Some changes go back, and some stay changed
explanations.definition: A change that can be undone is a reversible change. A change that cannot be undone is an irreversible change.
explanations.description: Melting and setting can go back and forth. Ice melts into water and freezes into ice again. Other changes make something new. Cooked rice will not turn back into raw rice, even when it is cold. Curd will not turn back into milk.
examples: Goes back: melted chocolate sets again in the fridge.
Stays changed: a chapati cooked on a tawa cannot become dough again.
Goes back: steam from a pressure cooker turns into water drops on a cold lid.
explanations.context: This card helps you sort the changes you have seen.
explanations.art: A two-sided chart: on the left a circle of arrows between ice and water, on the right a one-way arrow from dosa batter to a dosa.

agreed.text: Heat makes the starch in rice absorb water and swell. This is why cooked rice is soft.
agreed.evidence: Rice soaked in cold water stays hard. The same rice boiled for the same time goes soft. Under a microscope, starch grains in hot water swell and burst.

agreed.text: Curd is made by bacteria, not by the milk alone.
agreed.evidence: Warm milk with a spoon of curd sets by morning. The same milk with nothing added, or with boiled curd, does not set the same way. Under a microscope, curd is full of bacteria.

agreed.text: Ghee is butter with its water boiled away.
agreed.evidence: Butter in a hot pan fizzes and gives off steam until the bubbling stops. The ghee left over weighs less than the butter did, because the water has gone.

challenging.claim: Cooking takes all the goodness out of food.
challenging.who: Some people who eat only raw food
challenging.for: Long boiling does lose some vitamin C from vegetables into the water.
challenging.against: Cooking makes rice, dal and many other foods soft enough to digest, and boiling kills most germs. Raw rice and raw dal are very hard for our bodies to use. Steaming, or cooking vegetables for a short time, keeps most of their vitamins.
challenging.context: This card is about a claim you may hear about cooking.

challenging.claim: Soaking rice before cooking makes it cook faster.
challenging.for: Soaked grains already have some water inside, so the heat has less work to do.
challenging.against: The time saved is a few minutes, and it depends on the kind of rice.
challenging.context: This card is about soaking rice before cooking.

challenging.claim: Learning to cook changed the bodies of our human ancestors.
challenging.who: Richard Wrangham, a scientist who studies chimpanzees and human evolution
challenging.for: Cooked food is soft and easy to digest. Wrangham says this let our ancestors grow smaller teeth and guts, and bigger brains.
challenging.against: Other scientists say the oldest signs of cooking fires are too few to be sure people cooked that long ago. They say eating meat, or cutting food with stone tools, may matter more.
challenging.context: This card is about a big idea scientists still argue about.

big_questions.q: Melted butter set again, but ghee never became butter again. When does a thing stop being itself and become something new?
big_questions.hint: Think about butter, ghee, milk and curd. Which ones still have the same parts inside?

big_questions.q: Bacteria set the curd while you slept. Who made the curd: you, or the bacteria?
big_questions.hint: Think about who stirred in the curd, who did the changing, and who ate it.

big_questions.q: Could anything change and then go back to exactly how it was, with nothing at all different?
big_questions.hint: Look closely at melted butter after it sets again. Is it exactly the same?

big_questions.q: A spoon of curd can turn a whole bowl of milk into curd. How can something so small change something so big?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the bacteria do while the milk is warm.

story.title: Too Much Rice for the Pot
story.note: Meenakshi, her father and her Paati are made up. Rice really does swell to about three times its dry size when it cooks, and boiling rice in a small, full pot really does froth over.
text: Meenakshi was seven. She lived with her Appa and her Paati in a flat in Madurai, on the third floor. Paati was her grandmother. Paati cooked lunch every day, and Meenakshi liked to stand beside her and watch.
One Saturday, Paati went to Chennai for a wedding. 'Appa will cook lunch today,' she said on her way out. 'Help him, kanna.'
Appa had never cooked rice before. He found the rice tin. He found a small steel pot. He poured in rice until the pot was half full. Then he poured in water, right up to the top.
'That is a lot of rice,' said Meenakshi.
'We are hungry,' said Appa. 'And this pot is just the right size. Look, it all fits.'

Meenakshi looked at the pot. She remembered something Paati always did. Paati used a big pot for only a little rice. Meenakshi had once asked her why. Paati had said, 'Rice grows, kanna. Give it room.'
'Appa,' said Meenakshi. 'Paati says rice grows. She says to give it room.'
Appa laughed. 'Rice is not a plant in a pot of soil. It cannot grow in a kitchen.' He put the pot on the stove and lit the gas.
Meenakshi was not sure. So she did a small test of her own. She took two grains of rice from the tin. She laid them on a plate. Then she waited.
After a while, the pot began to bubble. White froth climbed up the sides. It rose to the rim, and then it spilled over. It hissed on the hot stove.
'Aiyo!' said Appa. He turned the gas down low. He lifted the lid. The rice had swollen right up to the top of the pot. There was hardly any water left. The rice was pushing at the lid.
'Where has all the water gone?' said Appa. 'I filled it right to the top.'

Meenakshi took a spoon. She scooped out two cooked grains and put them on the plate next to her two dry grains. The cooked grains were fat and white and soft. They were much longer than the dry ones. She pressed one. It squashed flat.
'Look, Appa,' she said. 'The rice drank the water. That is why the water is gone. And that is why the rice is bigger.'
Appa looked at the four grains for a long time. 'So Paati was right,' he said. 'Rice does grow. It grows by drinking.'

They moved half the rice into a big pot, with more water, and let it finish cooking. The pot did not spill again. When it was done, Meenakshi counted the cups of cooked rice. Appa had put in two cups of dry rice. Now there were six cups of cooked rice.
'Six!' said Appa. 'We will eat rice until Monday.'
That evening Paati phoned from Chennai. 'How was lunch?' she asked.
'Appa made enough rice for the whole building,' said Meenakshi. 'I told him rice grows. Rice drinks the water, Paati. Then it gets fat.'
Paati laughed so hard she had to sit down. 'Next time,' she said, 'you show Appa how much to use. One cup of rice for two people. And a big pot.'
The next day, they took the extra rice down to their neighbour, Farzana Aunty, who made lemon rice with it for the children. Meenakshi stood beside her and watched.
'Farzana Aunty,' she said, 'did you know rice drinks water?'
'I did,' said Farzana Aunty. 'Did you know it drinks much more when the water is hot?'
Meenakshi did not know that. She decided to test it next.
story.epiphany: Rice does not just sit in the water. It drinks the water, and that is why cooked rice is bigger, softer and heavier than dry rice.
ask: Why did the water in Appa's pot disappear?
What was Meenakshi's small test, and what did it show?
How could Meenakshi test Farzana Aunty's idea, that rice drinks more water when the water is hot?

games.title: Can It Go Back? A card sorting game
games.context: This is a sorting game about kitchen changes. Each card names a change. Players decide if the change can go back, then turn the card over to check.

printables.title: 16 kitchen change cards to cut out

items.b: Goes back. Melted butter sets again when it is cold.

items.f: Chocolate melts in a hot hand

items.b: Goes back. In the warm, it turns clear and runny again.
Goes back. Warm the jar and the ghee is runny again.

items.f: Steam from the cooker turns into drops on the lid
items.b: Goes back. Heat the drops, and they turn into steam again.

items.f: Water turns to ice in the freezer
items.b: Goes back. The ice melts into water again.

items.f: Ice cream melts in a bowl
items.b: Goes back, but not perfectly. It freezes again, but turns hard and icy.
Stays changed. The grains have absorbed water, and cold will not make them raw again.
Stays changed. Bacteria made the milk sour and thick.

items.f: Dosa batter cooks into a dosa
items.b: Stays changed. A dosa cannot turn back into batter.

items.f: Chapati dough cooks on a tawa
items.b: Stays changed. A chapati cannot become dough again.
Stays changed. The water inside turned to steam and burst each kernel open.

items.f: Butter is heated until it becomes ghee
items.b: Stays changed. The water boiled away as steam, so it cannot be butter again.

items.f: Onion is fried until it turns brown

rules: Draw a line down the middle of a big sheet. On the left, draw a circle of two arrows and write Goes back. On the right, draw one arrow and write Stays changed.
Cut out the 16 cards. Mix them and stack them, words up.
Take turns. On your turn, read the top card aloud. Say Goes back or Stays changed, and why.
Turn the card over and read the back. If you were right, keep the card in front of you. A back that says 'but not perfectly' still counts as Goes back.
If you were wrong, put the card face up in the middle.
When the stack is empty, the player with the most cards wins. If two players tie, they both win.
Last, put every card on its right half of the mat, yours and the middle ones. Count each half.

flow.say: Look at the Stays changed half. How many of those use heat? Which ones were done by tiny living beings?
flow.kid: Count each half. Which has more?

Idli batter rising.

experiments.title: Ten Grains in a Line: what does cooking do to rice?
experiments.context: In this experiment you keep some rice grains dry, soak some in cold water and boil some. Then you line up ten grains of each kind and see which line is longest.
experiments.question: We keep ten rice grains dry, soak ten in cold water and boil some in hot water, for the same time. Which ten grains will make the longest line? Which will be soft?
experiments.predict: Will the soaked grains and the boiled grains make longer lines than the dry grains, shorter lines or the same? Which will be soft? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: All the grains come from the same packet of rice. The soaked grains and the boiled grains each get one cup of water and stay in it for the same 12 minutes. We line up ten whole grains of each kind, end to end, in the same way. Only one thing changes: no water, cold water or boiling water. So any difference comes from the water and the heat.
results_table: Length of the line of 10 grains

materials.item: rice, the kind your family eats, such as sona masoori, ponni, gobindobhog or basmati
2 small steel katoris
a small pan or steel vessel, and the stove, used by a grown-up
a tea strainer
a steel plate
a long strip of paper, cut from a notebook page or newspaper
a pencil and a ruler. If you have no ruler, use your finger-widths.
a phone timer or a clock

experiments.safety: A grown-up boils the water, adds the grains and pours them out. Let the boiled grains cool on the plate for two minutes before your child touches them.

schedule.what: Soak and boil the grains for 12 minutes, line up the dry grains while you wait, then line up and compare all three.

experiments.record: Draw or stick the three lines of ten grains on the paper strip. Write the length under each line, and the words hard or soft.

flow.do: 1. Put a spoon of rice on a steel plate. 2. Your child picks out 40 whole grains, not broken ones. 3. Make heaps of 10, 10 and 20.
flow.say: Look closely at one grain. Is it hard or soft? Hold it up to the light. Can you see light through it?
flow.kid: Pick out 40 whole grains. Make heaps of 10, 10 and 20. Feel one grain. Is it hard?
flow.parent: We boil 20 grains, because a few may break. You need ten whole ones at the end.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the katori of cold water and the pan. 2. Ask for a guess and a reason. 3. Write the guesses in the table.
flow.say: Ten grains stay dry. Ten go in cold water. Some go in boiling water. Which line of ten will be longest? Which grains will be soft? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Some grains stay dry. Some go in cold water. Some go in boiling water. Which will be longest? Why?

good: Water makes things soft, so both wet ones.
Hot water cooks the rice, so the boiled ones.
Rice does not change size, so all the same.

flow.parent: Every guess is fine. Many children think the soaked grains and the boiled grains will be the same, because both were in water.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up puts one cup of water on to boil in a small pan. It takes about 4 minutes. 2. When it bubbles, your child puts 10 grains in a katori with one cup of cold water. 3. At the same moment, the grown-up drops in the 20 grains. 4. Turn the gas down so the water keeps bubbling gently, and start a 12-minute timer.
flow.say: Both lots of grains go in water at the same moment. That way they get the same time in the water.
flow.kid: A grown-up drops the grains in boiling water. You put yours in cold water. Start the timer.
flow.parent: Keep the water bubbling gently. If it gets low, add a little more hot water. The grains must stay under water. Do the dry-grain line (next step) while the water heats and the timer runs.

flow.do: 1. Lay the 10 dry grains on the paper strip, end to end, touching. 2. Mark the start and end with a pencil. 3. Write Dry beside the line. 4. Measure the line, or count finger-widths.
flow.say: Put the grains in a straight line, each one touching the next. How long is the line of ten?
flow.kid: Put the dry grains in a line, touching. Mark both ends. How long is it?
flow.parent: Lay the grains lengthwise, tip to tip, like a train. A line of ten dry sona masoori grains is about 5 cm. Basmati is longer.

flow.do: 1. While the timer runs, your child draws one dry grain, large. 2. Next to it, they draw how they think a boiled grain will look.
flow.say: Draw a dry grain, big. Now draw what you think a boiled grain will look like. Will it be the same shape?
flow.kid: Draw a dry grain. Then draw how you think a boiled one will look.

flow.do: 1. When the timer rings, a grown-up pours the boiled grains through the tea strainer. 2. Spread them on the plate to cool. 3. Drain the soaked grains too.
flow.say: The boiled grains are hot. We wait two minutes before we touch them.
flow.kid: Wait two minutes. The boiled grains are hot.

flow.do: 1. Lay 10 soaked grains under the dry line, end to end, and mark the ends. 2. Do the same with 10 whole boiled grains. 3. Measure each line. 4. Press one grain of each kind between finger and thumb.
flow.say: Which line is longest now? Press one grain of each kind. Which ones squash? Which ones are white?
flow.kid: Make a line of soaked grains and a line of boiled grains. Which is longest? Squash one of each.
flow.parent: Expect the boiled line to be clearly longer, often about one and a half times the dry line. The soaked grains may turn a little whiter and grow only a little. They stay hard. If a boiled grain is bent, straighten it gently. Some kinds of rice need a few minutes longer than 12 to go fully soft. If the middle of a boiled grain is still hard, say so honestly. The boiled line is still the longest.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they think, what they saw and why. Then ask the questions below.
flow.say: What do you think happened to the boiled grains? What did you see? Why did they grow more than the soaked ones?
flow.kid: Say what happened. Say what you saw. Say why you think so.

ask.q: Where did the extra length come from?
good: The grains drank the water.
Water went inside the grains.

ask.q: Both lots were in water for 12 minutes. Why did the boiled ones grow more?
good: The heat let more water in.
Hot water goes in better than cold water.

check.q: Which grains made the longest line?
options: The grains soaked in cold water
check.why: Heat loosens the packed starch inside each grain. Then water can go deep inside, and the grain swells long and soft. In cold water, only a little water gets in.

flow.parent: This is the heart of the unit. The only difference between the soaked and the boiled grains was heat. So heat is what let the water go deep inside.

experiments.title: How Much Water Does Rice Drink?
experiments.context: In this experiment two pans get the same amount of water. One pan gets some rice too. After 12 minutes you count the spoons of water left in each pan.
experiments.question: When rice cooks, the water in the pan goes down. How much does the rice drink, and how much goes off as steam?
experiments.predict: Both pans start with 8 spoons of water. Which pan will have less water left? About how many spoons less? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Both pans are the same size and get the same 8 tablespoons of water. Both are brought to a gentle boil, then kept on low heat with the lid on, for the same 12 minutes. Only one thing changes: one pan also has 2 tablespoons of rice. Steam leaves both pans. So the extra water missing from the rice pan is the water the rice drank.
results_table: Spoons of water at the start

materials.item: 2 small pans or steel vessels of the same size, with lids
a tablespoon
rice
water
a tea strainer and a small katori
the stove, used by a grown-up

experiments.safety: A grown-up does the boiling and pours out the hot water. Let the pans cool for five minutes before the water is poured out.

schedule.what: Boil two pans of water for 12 minutes, one with rice in it, then count the spoons of water left in each.

experiments.record: Draw the two pans. Under each one, draw a spoon for every spoonful of water left.

setup.art: Two small steel pans side by side, a child pouring a tablespoon of water into one, with a tally of 8 marks on a paper beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Put 8 spoons of water in each pan. Add 2 spoons of rice to one.

setup.art: Both pans on two burners of a gas stove, lids on, a little steam escaping.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up boils both, lids on, for 12 minutes.

setup.art: A grown-up pouring the water from the rice pan through a tea strainer into a katori, and a child counting spoonfuls from the katori.
setup.caption: 3. Pour out the water left in each pan. Count the spoons.

flow.do: 1. Your child counts 8 tablespoons of water into each pan. 2. They add 2 tablespoons of rice to one pan. 3. Label the pans Water and Rice.
flow.say: Count eight spoons into each pan. Fill each spoon to the top, so the pans get the same.
flow.kid: Put 8 spoons of water in each pan. Add 2 spoons of rice to one.

flow.do: Ask for a guess and a reason. Write it down.
flow.say: Both pans start with eight spoons. Which one will have less left? How many spoons less? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which pan will have less water left? Why?

good: The rice will drink some.
Steam will take some from both.
They will be the same, because both boil.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up brings both pans to a gentle boil, then turns the heat low, lids on. 2. Keep them bubbling gently for 12 minutes. 3. Turn off the gas and let the pans cool for 5 minutes.
flow.say: Both pans lose some water as steam. Watch the lids. Can you see steam coming out of both?
flow.kid: A grown-up boils both pans. Look for steam from both lids.
flow.parent: If you have only one burner, boil the water-only pan first, then the rice pan, for the same time. While you wait, your child can draw the two pans.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up pours the water from the water-only pan into a katori. 2. Your child counts the spoonfuls. 3. Do the same with the rice pan, through the tea strainer.
flow.say: Count the spoons of water left in each pan. Write the numbers down.
flow.kid: Count the spoons of water left in each pan.
flow.parent: The water from the rice pan will be a little cloudy and thick. That is starch from the rice. Count it as water. Expect the rice pan to have about 3 or 4 spoons fewer.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they think, what they saw and why.
flow.say: Steam took water from both pans. So why did the rice pan lose more?
flow.kid: Which pan lost more water? Why?

ask.q: How many spoons did the rice drink?
good: The extra spoons missing from the rice pan.
For example, 6 gone minus 2 gone is 4 spoons.

check.q: Why did the rice pan lose more water than the water-only pan?
options: The rice drank some of the water
The rice pan had a hole
check.why: Steam left both pans. The rice pan lost extra water because the grains absorbed it. That water is now inside the cooked rice.

activities.title: Melt It or Make Ghee? Two spoons of butter
activities.context: In this activity you melt one spoon of butter gently and cool it again. A grown-up heats a second spoon on the stove until it becomes ghee. Then you see which one turns back into butter.

materials.item: butter, homemade or from a packet
2 small steel katoris
a bowl of hot water from the stove, about as hot as tea
a small kadai or pan, a spoon and the stove, used by a grown-up
the freezer or fridge

activities.safety: Hot ghee can burn badly. Only a grown-up heats the butter and pours the ghee. Your child watches from an arm's length away.

schedule.what: Melt one spoon of butter and make ghee from the other, cool both, then compare them.

activities.record: Draw the two katoris after they cool. Label one butter and one ghee. Write one word for how each one smells.

setup.art: A steel katori with a spoon of butter in it, floating in a bowl of hot water, with the butter turning to yellow liquid.
setup.caption: 1. Melt one spoon of butter in a katori floating in hot water.

setup.art: A grown-up stirring butter in a small kadai on a low flame, with small bubbles and white foam on top.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up heats the other spoon until it stops bubbling.

setup.art: Two katoris side by side: pale yellow butter that has set again, and golden ghee with tiny brown bits at the bottom.
setup.caption: 3. Cool both. Which one is butter again?

flow.do: 1. Put one spoon of butter in a katori. Keep the second spoon for the stove. 2. Your child looks at, smells and touches the butter with a clean finger. 3. Ask for a guess.
flow.say: One spoon we melt gently, then cool. One spoon I heat on the stove for longer. When they cool, will both be butter again? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the butter. Smell it. Will both spoons turn back into butter? Why?

good: Melted things go solid again in the fridge.
Cooking changes things, so the stove one will be different.

flow.do: 1. Stand the katori in the bowl of hot water. Do not let water get inside it. 2. Watch the butter melt. 3. Look for a clear yellow part and some white cloudy bits.
flow.say: Watch the edges first. What colour is the melted butter? Can you see some white bits?
flow.kid: Watch the butter melt. What colours can you see?
flow.parent: Butter is mostly fat, with some water and milk bits. When it melts, the white milk bits show up in the clear yellow fat.

flow.do: Put the melted butter katori in the freezer, or in the fridge.
flow.say: Now we make it cold. Let's see if it sets again.
flow.kid: Put the melted butter in the freezer.
flow.parent: In the freezer it sets in about 10 minutes. The fridge takes about 20.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up heats the second spoon of butter in a small kadai on low heat. 2. Your child listens and watches from an arm's length. 3. When the fizzing goes quiet and the bits at the bottom turn light brown, turn off the gas. 4. Pour the ghee into the second katori.
flow.say: Listen. Can you hear it fizzing? Bubbles are coming up. What do you think is leaving the butter?
flow.kid: Listen to the butter fizz. Watch the bubbles. What smell comes now?

good: Water boiling.
Steam coming out.
Something leaving the butter.

flow.parent: A spoon of butter takes about 3 to 5 minutes on low heat. The fizzing is the water in the butter boiling into steam. When the water is gone, it goes quiet. Turn off the gas at once, before the brown bits turn dark.

flow.do: 1. Let the ghee cool for 2 minutes. 2. Put it in the freezer next to the butter. 3. While you wait, look at the brown bits at the bottom of the ghee and smell it.
flow.say: Look at the brown bits in the ghee. They are the milk parts of the butter. Smell it. Is it the same smell as the butter?
flow.kid: Look at the ghee. What do the brown bits look like?

flow.do: 1. Take out both katoris. 2. Your child looks at, smells and gently presses each one. 3. Ask them to say what they think, what they saw and why.
flow.say: Which one is butter again? What is different about the other one? Smell them both.
flow.kid: Which one is butter again? Smell both. How are they different?

check.q: Why can ghee not turn back into butter?
options: The water in the butter boiled away as steam
Ghee is made from a different milk
check.why: Butter has some water mixed in. Heated for longer, that water boils away as steam, and the milk bits brown. Cooling does not bring the water back, so the ghee stays ghee.

flow.parent: The gently melted butter sets solid and pale yellow again. It may look a little different, with a thin watery layer underneath. The ghee may stay soft or set grainy, it is golden, has brown bits and smells nutty. Both are worth eating with rice afterwards.

activities.title: Milk and Curd: what changed overnight?
activities.context: In this activity you put milk and curd side by side and use your eyes, nose, tongue and a spoon to find every way they are different.

materials.item: boiled milk, cooled until it is just warm
a little curd in a katori
2 clean teaspoons

schedule.what: Compare milk and curd with your senses, then hear who made the change.

activities.record: Draw the two katoris tipped to one side. Write one word for the taste of each.

setup.art: Two steel katoris side by side, one of milk and one of curd, each with a teaspoon.
setup.caption: 1. Put milk and curd side by side.

setup.art: A child tipping the katori of curd sideways, and the curd staying in place.
setup.caption: 2. Tip each katori a little. Then taste each one.

flow.do: 1. Your child tips each katori a little. 2. They lift a spoonful of each and let it drop. 3. They smell each one.
flow.say: Tip each katori. Which one moves? Lift a spoonful and let it drop. Now smell them.
flow.kid: Tip each katori. Which one stays still? Smell both.

flow.do: Your child tastes a little of each, with a clean spoon each time.
flow.say: Taste the milk. Now taste the curd. Which one is sour?
flow.kid: Taste each one. Which one is sour?

flow.do: Ask what changed the milk into curd. Then tell them about the bacteria.
flow.say: Nobody cooked this curd. Tiny living beings called bacteria did the work. They ate the sugar in the milk and made it sour and thick. How could they do that without a stove?
flow.kid: Bacteria made the curd. They are tiny living beings. They ate the milk sugar. That made the milk thick and sour.

check.q: Who turned the milk into curd?
check.why: Bacteria from a spoon of curd feed on the milk sugar and make an acid. The acid makes the milk sour and thick.

flow.parent: Curd can never turn back into milk. This is a change that stays.

flow.do: Tonight, stir one teaspoon of curd into a katori of warm milk. Cover it and leave it somewhere warm until morning. Compare it with plain milk.
flow.say: Tonight we set our own curd. Tomorrow we will see if the bacteria did their work.
flow.kid: Stir a spoon of curd into warm milk. Leave it overnight.
flow.parent: On a cold night, wrap the katori in a cloth. It may take until the next afternoon to set.

activities.title: Kitchen Change Hunt
activities.context: In this activity you watch someone cook a meal and spot every change you can. Then you decide which changes can go back.

materials.item: paper and a pencil
a family member cooking a meal

activities.safety: Stand an arm's length away from the stove, hot oil and pressure cooker.

schedule.what: Watch a meal being cooked and write or draw every change.

activities.record: A list of the changes you spotted, each with a tick for goes back or a cross for stays changed.

setup.art: A child standing an arm's length from a stove, holding a paper and pencil, watching a woman fry onions.
setup.caption: 1. Watch someone cook. Spot every change.

setup.art: A child's list with small drawings: onion turning brown with a cross, steam on a lid with a tick.
setup.caption: 2. Tick the ones that can go back.

flow.do: Your child watches a meal being cooked. They draw or write each change they see, hear or smell.
flow.say: Tell me every change you see. What did it look like before? What does it look like now?
flow.kid: Watch the cooking. Draw each change you see.
flow.parent: Good ones to point out: onions going soft and brown, mustard seeds popping in oil, dal going soft, dosa batter turning firm, water drops on a lid.

flow.do: 1. Read through the list together. 2. For each change, your child decides: can it go back? 3. Tick or cross.
flow.say: Can a brown onion turn white again? Can the water drops on the lid turn back into steam?
flow.kid: Can each change go back? Tick it if yes.

ask.q: Which of your changes can go back?
good: The steam drops on the lid.
Ghee melting.
Ice melting.

activities.title: One Cup In, How Many Cups Out?
activities.context: In this activity you measure the dry rice your family cooks for a meal, then count how many cups of cooked rice it makes.

materials.item: a steel tumbler or cup
the rice your family cooks for one meal
a big spoon and a big bowl

activities.safety: A grown-up opens the pressure cooker or hot pot and spoons out the rice.

schedule.what: Measure the dry rice before cooking, then count the cooked rice after.

activities.record: Draw the tumblers of dry rice and the tumblers of cooked rice in two rows.

setup.art: A child filling a steel tumbler with dry rice from a tin, levelling the top with a finger.
setup.caption: 1. Count the tumblers of dry rice your family cooks.

setup.art: A grown-up spooning cooked rice into a tumbler, with three full tumblers lined up beside it.
setup.caption: 2. After cooking, count the tumblers of cooked rice.

flow.do: Before cooking, your child measures the dry rice with a tumbler, levelling each one off.
flow.say: How many tumblers of dry rice are we cooking? How many tumblers of cooked rice do you think we will get? Why?
flow.kid: Count the tumblers of dry rice. Guess how many cooked ones.

ask.q: How many tumblers of cooked rice will we get?
good: More, because rice grows.
The same.

flow.do: 1. After cooking, a grown-up spoons the cooked rice into the tumbler. 2. Fill it loosely, without pressing. 3. Your child counts the tumblers.
flow.say: How many tumblers now? Where did the extra come from?
flow.kid: Count the tumblers of cooked rice. Where did the extra come from?
flow.parent: One tumbler of dry rice usually makes about three tumblers of cooked rice. The water you cooked it in is now inside the grains.

projects.title: My Kitchen Change Diary
projects.context: In this project you draw one food change from your kitchen every day for five days. You draw the food before and after, and say what changed it.

materials.item: 5 notebook pages or sheets of paper
pencils and crayons

schedule.what: Draw one food before and after cooking. Write what changed it.
Draw the last change. Then lay out all five pages and count how many can go back.

projects.record: Five pages, each with a before drawing, an after drawing and one word: heat, cold, water or bacteria.

setup.art: A notebook page split in two: on the left a drawing of dosa batter in a bowl, on the right a drawing of a dosa, with an arrow between them.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the food before and after.

setup.art: Five notebook pages laid out in a row, each with a before and after drawing and a tick or a cross.
setup.caption: 2. After five days, count the ticks.

flow.do: Each day, your child chooses one change from the day's cooking. They draw it before and after, and write what changed it.
flow.say: What changed in the kitchen today? Draw it before and after. Was it heat, cold, water or bacteria?
flow.kid: Pick one change today. Draw before and after. What changed it?

flow.do: On day 5, lay out all five pages. Your child ticks the ones that can go back.
flow.say: How many of your five changes can go back? Which change surprised you most?
flow.kid: Which changes can go back? Count them.

good: Any change with a reason, for example popcorn, because it was so much bigger.

challenges.title: Set the Butter Fast, Without the Fridge
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. Can you make melted butter set again quickly, without putting it in the fridge or freezer?
challenges.problem: A grown-up melts four spoons of butter: three for the three ways below and one for your own idea. Find the fastest way to make melted butter set solid again, without putting it in the fridge or freezer.
constraints: The butter itself does not go in the fridge or freezer.
Use only things from home. Ice cubes are allowed.
Start all your tries with the same amount of melted butter, one spoon each.
materials: 4 spoons of butter, melted in katoris standing in hot water
steel katoris, a steel plate and a plastic box lid
a bowl of cold water, and ice cubes from the freezer
a piece of cardboard to wave as a fan
general: Stand the katori in a bowl of cold water with ice cubes.
Spread the butter thin on a steel plate, so more of it touches the cold metal.
Wave a piece of cardboard over the katori.
creative: Use a steel katori, not a plastic one. Steel takes heat away faster.
Add a pinch of salt to the ice water. Salty ice water gets colder than plain ice water.
Do two at once, so you can compare which way wins.
challenges.your_turn: Now try your own idea. Time how long your butter takes to set. Draw your best way and write the time.

setup.art: Three steel katoris of melted yellow butter on a table: one in a bowl of cold water, one spread on a steel plate, one with a child waving cardboard over it.
setup.caption: 1. Try three ways to cool the melted butter.

setup.art: A child pressing a spoon onto butter that has set solid on a steel plate, and a phone timer beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Press with a spoon to test. Time which one sets first.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up melts the butter in katoris standing in hot water. 2. Your child chooses three ways to cool it.
flow.say: Today the butter cannot go in the fridge. How could we make it set fast? What takes heat away?
flow.kid: How can you make the butter set fast, without the fridge?

flow.do: 1. Start all three at the same time. 2. Every two minutes, press each one gently with a clean spoon. 3. Write the time when each one is firm.
flow.say: Which one do you think will set first? Why? Press each one every two minutes.
flow.kid: Start all three. Press each one every two minutes.
flow.parent: On a hot day, plain tap water may be too warm to set butter, so use ice. A thin layer on a steel plate, or a steel katori in ice water, usually sets first. Waving cardboard alone is slow, and may not work at all in summer.

flow.do: Your child says which way won and why. Then they try their own idea with the fourth spoon.
flow.say: Which way set first? Why do you think it worked best?
flow.kid: Which way won? Why? Now try your own idea.

good: The cold water took the heat away.
Thin butter cools faster.
Steel gets cold fast.

challenges.safety: A grown-up melts the butter and carries the hot water. Keep the fourth katori in the hot water until you need it.

videos.check: Find a short, accurate video. Check it shows swelling starch, and does not say the water simply disappears.

quiz.p: Ten dry rice grains and ten boiled grains are lined up end to end. Which line is longer?
quiz.why: Boiled grains absorb water and swell, so each one is longer. If you chose the same, try lining them up yourself.

quiz.p: Some grains sat in cold water and some in boiling water, for 12 minutes each. Which grains stayed hard?
quiz.why: In cold water only a little water gets in. Heat lets water go deep inside the grain, which makes it soft.

quiz.p: Where does most of the water in a pan of cooking rice go?
opts: Through the bottom of the pan
Nowhere, it is still in the pan
quiz.why: The grains absorb it. Some water also leaves as steam, but most of it ends up inside the rice.

quiz.p: Divya, a girl of 8, melts a spoon of butter in warm water, then puts it in the freezer. What will she find after 10 minutes?
quiz.why: Melting can go back. When butter gets cold, its fat sets solid again.

quiz.p: Butter in a hot pan fizzes and bubbles. What is the fizzing?
opts: Water in the butter boiling into steam
quiz.why: Butter has some water mixed in. When it boils, it leaves as steam and makes the fizzing sound.

quiz.p: What turns warm milk into curd overnight?
quiz.why: Bacteria from the spoon of curd feed on the milk sugar and make an acid that thickens the milk.
As the bacteria feed on milk sugar, they make an acid. Acids taste sour, like lemon juice.

opts: A dosa cooking on a tawa
quiz.why: Put the water in the freezer and it turns back into ice. A dosa and curd stay changed.

opts: Coconut oil going solid in the cold
quiz.why: Popcorn cannot turn back into hard kernels. Coconut oil and chocolate can melt and set again.

quiz.p: In the ten-grain test, why did we use ten grains in a line, not just one?
opts: One grain is too small to see
A line of ten shows the difference more clearly
quiz.why: One grain grows only a few millimetres. Ten grains add up, so the difference between the lines is easy to see and measure.

quiz.p: In the ten-grain test, the soaked and the boiled grains stayed in water for the same time. Why?
opts: So that only the heat was different
quiz.why: If only one thing changes, we know that thing made the difference. Here it was the heat.

items.p: Remember the ten-grain test? Which grains turned soft?
items.why: Boiled grains absorbed lots of water and swelled. They squash flat between your fingers.

items.p: Rice soaked in cold water for 12 minutes goes as soft as boiled rice.
items.why: False. Soaked grains may turn a little whiter and grow a little, but they stay hard. Heat is needed to let the water go deep inside.

items.p: Draw a line from each food to what it becomes.
items.why: Each food on the left changes into the one on the right when it is cooked or set.

items.p: Sort these changes: can they go back, or do they stay changed?
items.why: Melting and freezing can go back. Cooking rice and chapati, and setting curd, make something new that cannot go back.

items.p: When butter gets warm, it ______. When it gets cold again, it ______.
items.why: Butter is mostly fat. Fat melts when warm and sets solid when cold.

items.p: Say it out loud, and a grown-up writes it: where did the water in the rice pan go?
items.a: Most of it went inside the rice grains. Some went into the air as steam.
items.why: A strong answer says the grains absorbed the water, and may add that some left as steam.

items.p: Three of these changes stay changed. Which one can go back?
items.why: Melted ice freezes back into ice. Rice, dosa and curd stay changed.

items.p: Here is a pan of rice cooking. Label the steam, the water and the rice grains.
items.a: Steam above the pan, water in the pan, grains in the water.
items.why: Steam is water that has turned into a gas and floats up. The grains sit in the water and drink it.
items.art: A pan on a stove with steam rising, water inside and grains of rice in the water, with three empty label boxes.

items.p: Kavya, a girl of 8, and her brother Arjun, who is 6, melted some butter. Then they put it in the freezer, and it set again.

views.says: It is solid butter again. So nothing changed.
It looks a little different now. There is a watery layer underneath. So it did change a bit.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason. For example: 'Arjun, because it is butter and it is solid again.' Then it is fair to Kavya: it may look a little different, because the water and milk bits settled.
items.why: Both are partly right. The fat melted and set again, so that part went back. But the water and milk bits may have moved, so it is not exactly the same as before.

items.p: A grown-up melts butter in a katori. What will make it set solid again?
items.why: Butter is mostly fat. Fat sets solid when it gets cold.

worksheets.title: Heat, water and tiny living beings

items.p: Why did the boiled grains grow more than the soaked grains?
opts: Heat let the water go deep inside
The soaked grains were smaller to start with
items.why: Heat loosens the packed starch inside the grain. Then much more water can get in.

items.p: Put these in order, to make ghee from butter.
items.why: First the fat melts. Then the water boils away with a fizz. When the water has gone, it goes quiet, and the milk bits turn brown.

items.p: Anjali, a girl of 7 in Kochi, cooked rice. The pan had no water left. Her cousin said, 'All the water turned to steam.' What else happened to the water?
items.a: The rice grains drank most of it.
items.why: A strong answer says that some water left as steam, but most of it went inside the grains. The two-pan test shows this.

items.p: You can turn curd back into milk by stirring it hard.
items.why: False. Stirring makes curd runny, but it is still sour curd. The bacteria have changed the milk for good.

items.p: Divya, a girl of 8, and her friend Farhan, who is 8 too, are eating curd rice.

views.says: Rice is a food. You chew it, so it is not a drink.
Cooked rice is mostly water. So eating rice is a bit like drinking water.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason, for example: 'Farhan, because the rice drank two cups of water when it cooked.' Then it is fair to Divya: the water is held inside the grains, so you chew it as food.
items.why: Both are right in a way. Cooked rice is more than half water, so it does give your body water. But the water is held inside the soft grains, so we eat it as a food.

items.p: Draw the katori of melted butter before the freezer, and after.
items.a: A runny yellow puddle, then a solid pale yellow layer.
items.why: A strong drawing shows liquid butter with white bits first, then solid butter after, perhaps with a thin watery layer underneath.
items.art: Two empty katoris drawn side by side, labelled Before and After.

items.p: In the ten-grain test, we boiled 20 grains but only measured 10. Why did we start with extra?
items.a: Some grains may break in the water, and we need ten whole ones for a fair line.
items.why: A strong answer says broken grains cannot go in the line, so extra grains make sure there are ten whole ones.

items.p: A spoon of curd is stirred into warm milk. What does the spoon of curd bring to the milk?
items.why: The curd holds millions of bacteria. They feed on the milk sugar and multiply.

items.p: A change that can go back is called a ______ change.
items.why: Reversible means it can be undone. Melted butter setting again is a reversible change.

items.p: In the two-pan test, why did both pans get the same amount of water and the same time on the stove?
opts: So the steam lost from both pans would be about the same
So both pans would finish at the same time
Because the pans were the same colour
items.why: If both pans lose the same to steam, the extra water missing from the rice pan is what the rice drank.

items.p: Predict: if you boil rice grains for only 3 minutes, will the line of ten be as long as after 12 minutes? Why do you think so?
items.a: No, it will be shorter, because the grains will not have had time to absorb as much water.
items.why: A strong answer says water needs time to soak deep into the grain, so a short boil gives a shorter line. It may suggest testing it.

items.p: Two cooks make rice in different ways. Lakshmi Paati, in Chennai, soaks rice for 20 minutes before cooking. Mitali, in Kolkata, cooks it straight from the packet.

views.says: Soaking lets the water start going in. So the rice cooks faster and uses less gas.
In the morning rush, I have no time to wait 20 minutes. It only saves a few minutes anyway.

items.ask: Whose way would you choose? Why? Then say one thing the other cook has right.
items.a: A strong answer chooses a way and gives a reason, then is fair to the other cook. For example: 'Lakshmi Paati, because saving gas matters. But Mitali is right that soaking takes planning.'
items.why: This is a real trade-off. Soaking saves a few minutes of cooking and some gas. Not soaking saves planning time. Both are sensible.

items.p: Nila, a girl of 7, stirred curd into warm milk and left it in the fridge overnight. In the morning it was still runny. Why?
opts: The cold slowed the bacteria down
Curd only sets in the daytime
items.why: Bacteria in curd work best in warm milk. In the cold, they work very slowly, so the milk stays runny.

items.p: Draw what you think happens inside one rice grain when it is boiled. Show where the water goes.
items.a: A grain with water drops going into it and the inside swelling.
items.why: A strong drawing shows water moving from outside into the grain, and the grain getting bigger. Arrows pointing in are a good way to show it.

items.p: Three of these changes are done by heat. Which one is not?
items.why: Curd is set by bacteria, not by heat. Rice, popcorn and chapati change in a hot pan or on a tawa.

items.p: Find the mistake. Arjun, a boy of 6, says, 'Melted butter goes back when it is cold. So if I put cooked rice in the fridge, it will turn back into raw rice.' What is wrong?
items.a: Cooking rice is not like melting. The grains absorbed water and changed inside, and cold does not undo that.
items.why: A strong answer says that some changes go back and some do not. Melting can be undone by cold, but cooking makes a new thing, so cold rice is still cooked rice.

items.p: Sort these changes by what caused them: heat, cold or living beings.
items.why: Heat cooks the ghee and the dosa. Cold sets the ice and the coconut oil. Bacteria and other tiny living beings change milk and idli batter.

items.p: Here is a katori of homemade ghee. Label the golden ghee and the brown bits.
items.a: Golden ghee at the top, brown bits at the bottom.
items.why: The brown bits are the milk parts of the butter, browned by the heat. The golden part is the fat.
items.art: A steel katori of clear golden ghee with a scatter of brown bits at the bottom, and two empty label boxes.

items.p: Does more water in the pan make rice grains swell more? Say how you would test it fairly. What would you keep the same?
items.a: Cook the same rice for the same time in different amounts of water, and keep the pan, the heat and the time the same.
items.why: A strong answer changes only the amount of water and keeps the rice, pan, heat and time the same.

items.p: Ice cream that melted and froze again is exactly the same as before.
items.why: False. It freezes again, but it turns hard and icy. A change can go back and still leave something a little different.

applications: Cooks use the fact that rice grows about three times when they plan how much to cook for a wedding or a festival meal.
Dairies in India, like the milk cooperatives in Gujarat, make curd and buttermilk by adding the right bacteria to warm milk.
Ghee lasts for months without a fridge, because it has almost no water left in it for germs to grow in.
Food scientists study how cooking changes food. Kamala Sohonie, one of the first Indian women to earn a science PhD, studied the food value of neera, a drink tapped from palm trees.

open_questions.q: Did learning to cook change the bodies of our human ancestors?
open_questions.why_open: Some scientists think cooked food let our ancestors grow smaller teeth and bigger brains. Others say the signs of very old cooking fires are too few to be sure.

open_questions.q: How many kinds of bacteria live in homemade curd?
open_questions.why_open: Curd from different homes and towns holds different mixes of bacteria. Scientists are still studying them.

open_questions.q: When did people first cook rice?
open_questions.why_open: Rice was farmed in China and India thousands of years ago. But cooked rice rots quickly, so very old meals are hard to find. Scientists look for burnt grains in old cooking pots.

maths.problem: In the ten-grain test, the line of 10 dry grains was 5 cm long. The line of 10 boiled grains was 8 cm long. How much longer was the boiled line?
maths.explain: 8 take away 5 is 3. So the boiled line was 3 cm longer than the dry line.
maths.context: This is about the ten-grain test, where you lined up dry, soaked and boiled rice grains.
maths.why_maths: Taking one length from the other tells us exactly how much the grains grew.

maths.problem: One tumbler of dry rice makes about 3 tumblers of cooked rice. A cook is making rice for a family lunch with 3 tumblers of dry rice. About how many tumblers of cooked rice will there be?
maths.explain: Each tumbler of dry rice becomes 3 tumblers. 3 and 3 and 3 makes 9.
maths.context: This is about counting tumblers of rice before and after cooking.
maths.why_maths: Equal groups help a cook predict how much cooked rice there will be, before it is cooked.

maths.problem: In the two-pan test, both pans started with 8 spoons of water. The water-only pan had 6 spoons left. The rice pan had 2 spoons left. How many spoons did the rice drink?
maths.explain: The water-only pan lost 2 spoons, as steam. The rice pan lost 6 spoons. Steam took 2 of those, the same as the other pan. 6 take away 2 is 4. So the rice drank 4 spoons.
maths.context: This is about the two-pan test, where one pan of water had rice in it and one did not.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the two pans lets us take away the steam, so we can find just the water the rice drank.

maths.problem: Kavya, a girl of 8, watched a meal being cooked and found 7 changes. 2 could go back and 5 stayed changed. Make tally marks for each kind. Which kind did she find more of, and how many more?
maths.explain: Two tally marks for goes back, five for stays changed. 5 take away 2 is 3, so she found 3 more changes that stayed changed.
maths.context: This is about the kitchen change hunt, where you watched a meal being cooked.
maths.why_maths: Tally marks let us count each kind quickly and see which kind of change is more common in cooking.

science: Cooked white rice is about 68 to 70% water: USDA FoodData Central, rice, white, long-grain, regular, cooked. Raw rice is about 12% water.

Starch gelatinisation: starch granules absorb water and swell when heated above about 60 to 70 °C, while in cold water they take up only a little. Rice grains lengthen on cooking. Elongation ratios of about 1.3 to 2 are reported, highest in basmati types.
Butter is at least 80% milk fat and up to about 16% water (FSSAI standard for table butter). Ghee is made by heating butter until the water boils off and the milk solids brown.
Curd: lactic acid bacteria ferment lactose to lactic acid, which lowers the pH and makes the casein proteins gel. Their work slows greatly at fridge temperatures.

Louis Pasteur, 'Mémoire sur la fermentation appelée lactique', 1857. Justus von Liebig held that fermentation was a chemical breakdown, not the work of living cells. Stamen Grigorov described the bacterium later named Lactobacillus bulgaricus in 1905, in Geneva.
Richard Wrangham, Catching Fire: How Cooking Made Us Human, 2009. The cooking hypothesis is debated.
Kamala Sohonie: PhD from the University of Cambridge in 1939, among the first Indian women to earn a PhD in science. Later studied the nutrition of neera (palm sap).
Chandogya Upanishad 6.5.1: food when eaten becomes threefold. Bhagavad Gita 15.14: 'Becoming the fire of digestion in the bodies of living beings, I digest the four kinds of food.'

roots.context: We have watched rice grains grow in boiling water, butter turn into ghee, and milk become curd. Now we ask what cooking tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In cold water, your rice grains stayed hard and grew only a little. In boiling water, the same grains grew long and soft. Heat let the water go deep inside each grain. So most of a plate of cooked rice is the water you cooked it in.
deep_truth.habit: We think of rice as a dry food and water as a drink, two separate things on the table. But once rice is cooked, most of what we eat is water held inside the grains.
deep_truth.evidence: In the ten-grain test, boiled grains made a much longer line than soaked grains, though both sat in water for 12 minutes. In the two-pan test, the rice pan lost about 4 spoons more water than the water-only pan. One tumbler of dry rice makes about three of cooked rice.

three.who_am_i: Your body is mostly water, like cooked rice. The water in your food becomes part of you.
three.what_is_life: Curd bacteria change milk to feed themselves. Living beings are always changing their food, and being changed by it.
three.what_is_this_world: Some changes in the world go back, like melting. Many go only one way, like cooking.

roots.thread: Rice, water and heat sit on the stove as three separate things. In the pot, the water moves into the grain and the grain swells round it, until you cannot point to where the water is. From the same rice, water and heat, cooks make idli, dosa, pongal, payasam and pulao. Everything is conscious, down to the smallest particles, so the grain and the water take part in this change too. Many scientists see only particles moving and sticking.

teachings.teaching: Food, when it is eaten, is split three ways. The roughest part leaves the body, the middle part becomes flesh, and the finest part becomes mind.
teachings.link: Cooking is the first change food goes through. In the body it keeps changing, until it becomes part of you.

teachings.teaching: Krishna says he becomes the fire inside living bodies that digests their food.
teachings.link: Outside, the fire of the stove changes rice. Inside you, the body goes on changing it, and the Gita speaks of that as a fire too.

science.text: Heat makes the starch in rice absorb water and swell. Scientists call this gelatinisation.

other_view.view: They say a grain taking in water is only particles moving and sticking together. They see no need to say that the grain or the water takes part in anything.

practice.title: Feel the water in the grain
practice.say: Put one dry grain and one cooked grain on your palm. Close your eyes. Touch the dry grain with a fingertip. Now touch the cooked grain. Press it gently. Feel how soft and wet it is. That softness is the water from the pan. Now take one slow breath. Some of the water in your breath came from your food too.
practice.kid: Hold a dry grain and a cooked grain. Close your eyes. Touch each one. Which is soft? The water is inside it.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out who sets the curd? This card tells the true story.
how_we_found_out.story: For thousands of years, families in India, Bulgaria, Turkey and many other places set curd from a spoon of old curd. Nobody knew what really changed the milk. In the 1800s, a famous German chemist, Justus von Liebig, said that souring was only a chemical change, a kind of slow breaking down. He said no living thing was needed. In 1857, Louis Pasteur in France studied this souring closely. Under his microscope he found tiny living beings, much smaller than yeast. When he added a little of them to a fresh sugary liquid, that liquid turned sour too, and the tiny beings multiplied. So the souring was done by living microbes. In 1905, Stamen Grigorov, a young medical student from Bulgaria working in Geneva, looked at yogurt from his home country. He found a rod-shaped bacterium that makes milk thick and sour. It was later named Lactobacillus bulgaricus, after Bulgaria.
how_we_found_out.who: Louis Pasteur, a French chemist, and Stamen Grigorov, a Bulgarian medical student. Justus von Liebig, a German chemist, held the wrong idea.
how_we_found_out.when: Pasteur reported his work in 1857. Grigorov found the curd bacterium in 1905.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That milk and other foods turned sour by a chemical change alone, with no living thing involved. Pasteur showed the souring grew and spread only when the tiny living beings were there.
